def: Limited cutaneous systemic sclerosis: Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly and Telangiectasia. Associated with anti-centromere antibodies.
A common benign, waxy, stuck-on brown skin growth of older adults. Sudden eruption of many lesions (Leser-Trelat sign) can signal internal cancer.
Gastritis with markedly enlarged gastric folds. Includes Menetrier disease, with foveolar cell hyperplasia, protein-losing enteropathy and low acid output, and Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
Veins draining the intestines. The superior and inferior mesenteric veins join the splenic vein to form the portal vein; thrombosis causes bowel ischemia.
An enzyme that cross-links proteins. Tissue transglutaminase is the autoantigen targeted in celiac disease (anti-tTG IgA), where it deamidates gliadin.
Surgical removal of the colon and rectum, often with an ileal pouch-anal anastomosis, used for ulcerative colitis and familial adenomatous polyposis.
An abnormal connection between the bowel and another organ or the skin, such as colovesical or enterocutaneous. Common in Crohn disease and diverticulitis; colovesical fistula causes pneumaturia.
A common benign soft, movable tumor of fat cells under the skin.
A plant-derived reagent used in the fecal occult blood test; it turns blue when oxidized by the heme in blood.
A branch of the celiac trunk that runs along the pancreas to the spleen, also supplying the stomach and pancreas. Its aneurysm is the most common visceral aneurysm.
A liver and bile duct enzyme raised in cholestasis and with alcohol use. Helps confirm that a raised alkaline phosphatase is of liver rather than bone origin.
Clot in the cavernous sinus, usually from spread of facial or sinus infection through the ophthalmic veins. Causes headache, orbital swelling, and palsies of cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2 and VI.
Involuntary twisting of the neck with the head tilted to one side, from sternocleidomastoid spasm (cervical dystonia) or congenital shortening.
Encapsulated onion-like nerve endings in deep skin that detect vibration and pressure.
Imaging of veins after injecting contrast, historically used to diagnose deep vein thrombosis.
The positive-sense RNA coronavirus that causes COVID-19. It enters cells via spike protein binding to ACE2.
Inflammation of both brain and spinal cord, as in acute disseminated encephalomyelitis after infection or vaccination.
Inherited peripheral neuropathy, most often PMP22 duplication, causing distal muscle wasting, high arches and foot drop (inverted champagne bottle legs).
Genetic disorders with both nervous system and skin lesions, such as neurofibromatosis, tuberous sclerosis, Sturge-Weber and von Hippel-Lindau.
A benign peripheral nerve sheath tumor of Schwann cells and fibroblasts. Multiple neurofibromas indicate neurofibromatosis type 1.
Nearsightedness, where the eye focuses light in front of the retina so distant objects look blurry. Corrected with concave (minus) lenses.
Inherited degeneration of retinal photoreceptors, starting with rods, causing night blindness, tunnel vision and bone-spicule pigment deposits on the retina.
A bacterial protein that activates plasminogen to plasmin, used as a thrombolytic in myocardial infarction. Can cause allergic reactions.
An intermediate-acting benzodiazepine used for insomnia, acting at GABA-A receptors to increase chloride channel opening frequency.
A nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic that acts at the GABA-A receptor, used for insomnia. May cause complex sleep behaviors.
A mild bipolar-spectrum mood disorder with at least 2 years of alternating hypomanic and mild depressive symptoms that never meet full criteria for mania or major depression.
Chronic low mood on most days for at least 2 years, milder than major depression, with symptoms like poor appetite, low energy and hopelessness.
A synthetic opioid agonist. Its metabolite normeperidine can cause seizures, and with MAO inhibitors it can cause serotonin syndrome.
An opioid with mixed agonist-antagonist action: kappa agonist and mu partial agonist or antagonist. Used for pain and can precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients.
An SSRI used for depression and anxiety. Has the most anticholinergic effect and withdrawal symptoms of its class, and is linked to fetal cardiac malformations.
An SSRI used for depression. Higher doses prolong the QT interval.
A serotonin receptor, a Gi-coupled receptor, that is the target of buspirone. Presynaptic autoreceptors reduce serotonin release.
A selective MAO-B inhibitor that slows dopamine breakdown, used in Parkinson disease. At high doses it loses selectivity.
A partial agonist at serotonin 5-HT1A receptors used for generalized anxiety disorder. Not sedating and has no abuse potential.
An antiepileptic that blocks T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, used for absence seizures.
The compound in chili peppers that activates TRPV1 heat receptors. Applied topically it depletes substance P to relieve neuropathic pain.
Involuntary spasm of the pelvic floor muscles around the vagina that prevents penetration, causing painful or impossible intercourse.
An urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, worse at rest and in the evening, relieved by movement. Linked to iron deficiency; treated with dopamine agonists.
Compounds acting on CB1 and CB2 receptors, including THC from cannabis. Effects include euphoria, increased appetite, red eyes and dry mouth.
An observational study following groups defined by exposure over time to compare outcomes. Allows calculation of relative risk and incidence.
A benign inherited cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, with mild jaundice. Unlike Dubin-Johnson syndrome, the liver is not pigmented.
Kidney failure from intense renal vasoconstriction in advanced cirrhosis with ascites, with structurally normal kidneys. Urine sodium is very low.
A yellow-brown 'wear-and-tear' pigment of lipid and protein, accumulating in aging cells such as heart, liver and neurons.
A cellular process in which cytoplasmic components and organelles are enclosed in vesicles and degraded in lysosomes, recycling nutrients under stress.
An enzyme (muramidase) in tears, saliva and neutrophils that cleaves peptidoglycan, killing gram-positive bacteria.
An industrial chemical used to make PVC that causes hepatic angiosarcoma.
Folds of peritoneum draping the stomach and bowel. The greater omentum hangs from the stomach and walls off infection and inflammation.
Abdominal wall arteries. The inferior epigastric artery arises from the external iliac and forms the medial boundary of Hesselbach triangle; the superior arises from the internal thoracic.
Protrusion of bowel through the femoral canal, below the inguinal ligament. More common in women and at high risk of strangulation.
The antibody classes IgG, IgA, IgM, IgD and IgE, defined by their heavy chain. Class switching changes isotype but not antigen specificity.
Cells such as dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells that display peptides on MHC class II to helper T cells.
A Th2 cytokine promoting IgE class switching, mucus production and airway hyperreactivity in asthma and allergy.
Type IV hypersensitivity, mediated by T cells not antibodies and appearing 24 to 72 hours after exposure. Includes contact dermatitis, tuberculin skin test and graft rejection.
A new infection occurring during treatment of an existing one, often because antibiotics eliminated normal flora, as in C. difficile colitis or candidiasis.
Inflammation of serous membranes (pleura, pericardium, peritoneum), as in lupus.
A liver-made carrier of thyroxine and retinol-binding protein, also called prealbumin. Misfolded transthyretin forms amyloid in familial and senile amyloidosis.
A genus of gram-negative rods including B. cepacia, a pathogen in cystic fibrosis and chronic granulomatous disease, and B. pseudomallei, which causes melioidosis.
A family of signaling proteins that stimulate fibroblast proliferation, angiogenesis and bone growth. Gain-of-function FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia.
A signaling protein that drives new blood vessel growth, upregulated in tumors and in diabetic retinopathy. Blocked by bevacizumab.
A raised, thickened scar from excess collagen that stays within the original wound borders, unlike a keloid.
Chronic liver inflammation from autoimmunity, often in women, with elevated transaminases and antibodies such as ANA, anti-smooth muscle and anti-LKM1. Responds to steroids.
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry, the standard test of bone mineral density for osteoporosis. Results are given as T-scores.
A collapse of vertebral body height, usually from osteoporosis, causing back pain and kyphosis.
A rare benign bone-forming tumor of the spine, similar to but larger than an osteoid osteoma and not relieved by NSAIDs.
Stiffening or fusion of a joint by bone or fibrous tissue, as in ankylosing spondylitis.
Inflammation of hair follicles, appearing as small pustules. Usually from Staphylococcus aureus; hot tub folliculitis is from Pseudomonas.
Autoimmune patchy hair loss with smooth round bald patches and 'exclamation point' hairs, from T cell attack on hair follicles.
An atypical mole, larger and irregular in color and border, that can be a precursor to melanoma. Multiple lesions occur in familial atypical mole and melanoma syndrome.
A kinase inhibitor targeting mutated BRAF V600E, used in metastatic melanoma. May cause cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma.
Drugs that block platelet activation or aggregation, such as aspirin (COX inhibitor), clopidogrel (P2Y12 blocker) and abciximab (GP IIb/IIIa blocker).
A congenital absence of the normal anal opening because the anal membrane or canal fails to develop. Associated with VACTERL and Down syndrome.
An oral, acid-stable penicillin used for strep pharyngitis and mild infections.
A second-generation cephalosporin with anaerobic coverage including Bacteroides fragilis, used for intra-abdominal infection and surgical prophylaxis.
A monoclonal antibody against EGFR used in colorectal cancer without KRAS mutation. Causes acneiform rash.
Surgical removal of the bladder, done for muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
A chemical cautery agent used to stop nosebleeds and treat granulation tissue; once used in newborn eyes to prevent gonococcal conjunctivitis.
Surgical cutting of a sphincter muscle, such as the anal sphincter for fissures or the sphincter of Oddi to relieve biliary obstruction.
Antithyroid drugs (methimazole, propylthiouracil) that block thyroid peroxidase and thyroid hormone synthesis. Can cause agranulocytosis; PTU can cause liver failure.
Exercise-related pain along the inner shin from overuse of the tibia and attached muscles, commonly called shin splints.
One of several closely related forms of a protein produced from different genes or by alternative splicing, with distinct tissue distribution, like CK-MB.
A fluid-filled swelling in the popliteal fossa from synovial fluid herniating from the knee joint, often with knee arthritis. Rupture can mimic deep vein thrombosis.
Compression of the posterior tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus, causing burning pain and numbness on the sole of the foot.
An enzyme that converts uric acid to the more soluble allantoin. Humans lack it; recombinant form (rasburicase) treats tumor lysis syndrome.
X-ray imaging of the coronary arteries after injecting contrast through a catheter to find blockages.
Surgical removal of atherosclerotic plaque from the carotid artery to prevent stroke in symptomatic high-grade stenosis.
Severe peripheral artery disease with rest pain, nonhealing ulcers or gangrene from inadequate blood flow to the leg.
Liver abscess from Entamoeba histolytica spread from the colon, with fever and right upper quadrant pain; contents look like anchovy paste. Treated with metronidazole.
The infective stage of Plasmodium injected by a mosquito. They travel to the liver and invade hepatocytes.
A topical azole antifungal that inhibits ergosterol synthesis, used for candidiasis and tinea.
An antifungal converted by fungal cells to 5-fluorouracil, inhibiting DNA and RNA synthesis. Used with amphotericin B for cryptococcal meningitis; causes bone marrow suppression.
The encapsulated serotype causing meningitis, epiglottitis and sepsis in children. The Hib conjugate vaccine has made it uncommon.
An anaerobic gram-negative rod of the gut that causes intra-abdominal abscess and peritonitis. Treated with metronidazole.
The HIV gene encoding reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease.
Eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions in neurons, found in the hippocampus and Purkinje cells in rabies.
EDTA, a chelator that binds metal ions. Calcium disodium EDTA treats lead poisoning; EDTA in blood tubes prevents clotting by binding calcium.
An infection acquired in a hospital, often with resistant organisms, such as catheter-associated UTI, ventilator pneumonia and C. difficile.
Abnormally large brain with enlarged head size.
A neuraminidase inhibitor that blocks release of influenza virions from cells. Works best within 48 hours of symptoms.
An antiparasitic that opens glutamate-gated chloride channels, paralyzing worms. Treats strongyloidiasis, onchocerciasis, scabies and lice.
A once-daily carbapenem, not active against Pseudomonas or Enterococcus, used for intra-abdominal and complicated urinary infections.
Degenerative arthritis of the spine with disc narrowing and osteophytes, often in the neck, which can compress nerve roots.

A tick-borne infection by Anaplasma phagocytophilum, an obligate intracellular bacterium infecting neutrophils (morulae). Causes fever, leukopenia and elevated liver enzymes; treated with doxycycline.
A painless, firm lump in the eyelid from a blocked meibomian gland with lipogranulomatous inflammation.
Genus of hard ticks that transmit Lyme disease, anaplasmosis and babesiosis.
Human herpesvirus 3 causing chickenpox and later reactivating from dorsal root ganglia as shingles.
A defective RNA virus that needs hepatitis B surface antigen to replicate, causing coinfection or superinfection that worsens hepatitis B.
An RNA virus genus spread mainly by mosquitoes and ticks, including yellow fever, dengue, Zika, West Nile and hepatitis C viruses.
Clonal expansion of mast cells in tissues, often with a KIT D816V mutation, causing flushing, abdominal pain and anaphylaxis episodes. Tryptase is elevated.
A cytidine analog antimetabolite that inhibits DNA synthesis, used for pancreatic cancer and bladder cancer.
A nitrosourea alkylating drug toxic to pancreatic beta cells, used for islet cell tumors and to induce diabetes in animals.
The most common group of lung cancers, including adenocarcinoma, squamous cell carcinoma and large cell carcinoma. Distinct from small cell lung cancer.
Antifungal drugs such as terbinafine that inhibit squalene epoxidase and ergosterol synthesis, used for onychomycosis.
A malaria parasite causing fever every 72 hours (quartan). Associated with nephrotic syndrome.
The multinucleated stage of malaria parasites in liver or red cells that divides to release merozoites.
A nematode acquired from undercooked pork. Larvae encyst in muscle, causing periorbital edema, myalgias and eosinophilia.
The genus of roundworms causing trichinosis, acquired by eating undercooked meat. Larvae encyst in skeletal muscle.
E. coli strain causing traveler's diarrhea through heat-labile (increases cAMP) and heat-stable (increases cGMP) toxins.
A water-soluble oral contrast (diatrizoate) used for CT or imaging of bowel perforation or obstruction, where barium would be harmful.
Inflammation of the thick band of tissue on the sole, causing heel pain worst with the first steps in the morning.
Proteins that restrain cell division or promote apoptosis, such as p53 and Rb. Loss of both alleles contributes to cancer.
Autoimmune inflammation of the thyroid with lymphocytic infiltration, most commonly Hashimoto disease, causing hypothyroidism.
Subclavian artery stenosis proximal to the vertebral origin that reverses vertebral flow, causing arm ischemia and dizziness with arm exercise.
A broad, flat sheet of tendon connecting muscle to bone or other muscle.
Sweat glands in the armpits and genital area that open into hair follicles and secrete a milky fluid, giving rise to body odor.
Infection of the mastoid air cells behind the ear, usually as a complication of otitis media, with postauricular pain and swelling.
Inflammation of the glans penis, often from Candida in diabetics or poor hygiene.
Inflammatory lung disease with plugs of granulation tissue in airways and alveoli, with no known cause. Causes cough and dyspnea; responds to steroids.
A pattern of lung injury with granulation tissue plugs in small airways and alveoli, formerly called BOOP. Can be idiopathic or secondary to infection, drugs or autoimmune disease.
Needle drainage of fluid from the pericardial sac, used to treat cardiac tamponade.
Rigid extension of the arms and legs with arms pronated, from a brainstem lesion below the red nucleus.
Surgical opening of the skull to reach the brain.
The uterus turning inside out, usually after delivery from excessive cord traction, causing hemorrhage and shock.
Thinning and dryness of the vaginal lining from low estrogen after menopause, causing dyspareunia and irritation.

term: Atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance
def: The mildest abnormal Pap smear result, showing cell changes not clearly precancerous. Triaged with HPV testing.
Surgical or catheter removal of a blood clot from a vessel.
Inability to retract the foreskin over the glans penis because it is too tight.
An antibiotic used to differentiate Staphylococcus saprophyticus (resistant) from S. epidermidis (sensitive).
A gram-positive coccus that is a normal gut organism, causing urinary tract infection, endocarditis and biliary infection. Grows in bile and 6.5% salt; often vancomycin-resistant.
Sleeping sickness caused by Trypanosoma brucei from tsetse flies, causing fever, lymphadenopathy and later CNS disease with daytime sleep.
Enzymes that transfer an acetyl group onto a substrate. Examples are N-acetyltransferase for isoniazid metabolism and histone acetyltransferases for gene regulation.
Prostaglandin F2-alpha, used to induce labor or abortion and cause uterine contraction.
A cartilage flap that covers the larynx during swallowing. Inflammation (epiglottitis) causes stridor and drooling; the thumb sign on x-ray.
A high-potency typical antipsychotic that blocks D2 receptors, available as a long-acting depot injection.
A Gq-coupled receptor found in the CNS, stomach enterochromaffin-like cells and sympathetic ganglia. Pirenzepine is selective for it.
Malabsorption after loss of much of the small intestine, causing diarrhea, dehydration and nutrient deficiencies. Ileal loss causes B12 and bile acid deficiency.
A single long protein made from viral RNA that is cut by proteases into the individual functional proteins, as in HIV and hepatitis C.
An enzyme that breaks down cAMP or cGMP. PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil) raise cGMP; theophylline and caffeine inhibit PDE.
A receptor with intrinsic guanylyl cyclase activity that produces cGMP when bound, such as the ANP receptor.

An amino acid, a urea cycle intermediate made from ornithine and carbamoyl phosphate. Also produced when nitric oxide synthase converts arginine, and citrullinated proteins are autoantigens in rheumatoid arthritis.
The enzyme that makes nitric oxide from arginine, using oxygen and NADPH. Endothelial NOS produces NO for vasodilation.
Intracellular receptors that bind lipid-soluble hormones and act as transcription factors, including steroid, thyroid hormone, vitamin D and retinoic acid receptors.
Anterior pituitary cells that secrete growth hormone. Tumors cause acromegaly or gigantism.
A hypothalamic tripeptide that stimulates the pituitary to release TSH and prolactin.
Short chains of amino acids used as neurotransmitters or modulators, such as substance P, enkephalins and neuropeptide Y.
A tetracycline that blocks the effect of ADH on the collecting duct, used off-label for SIADH. Can cause nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
The main plasma carrier of thyroid hormones. Raised by estrogen, pregnancy and oral contraceptives, which raises total but not free T4.
The antibody to the TSH receptor in Graves disease that mimics TSH and drives thyroid hormone excess.
The adrenal zona glomerulosa enzyme (CYP11B2) that makes aldosterone from corticosterone.
A steroid intermediate in cortisol synthesis. Raised in 21-hydroxylase deficiency, so used to screen newborns for congenital adrenal hyperplasia.
Enzyme that converts cortisol to inactive cortisone in the kidney, protecting the mineralocorticoid receptor. Licorice inhibits it, causing hypertension and low potassium.
Drugs that mimic or enhance parasympathetic effects, such as pilocarpine, bethanechol and cholinesterase inhibitors.
An amino acid formed by vitamin C-dependent hydroxylation of proline in collagen. Its urinary excretion marks collagen breakdown.
Fluid-filled bone cavities beneath cartilage in osteoarthritis, alongside joint space narrowing, sclerosis and osteophytes.
Sudden hemorrhage or infarction of the pituitary, often in an adenoma, causing severe headache, vision loss and hypopituitarism.
Membrane water channels. Aquaporin-2 in the collecting duct is inserted in response to ADH.
Demyelination of the pons from overly rapid correction of hyponatremia, causing quadriparesis, dysarthria and locked-in syndrome.
Drugs that reduce thyroid hormone production, such as methimazole and propylthiouracil.
The urinary breakdown product of serotonin, raised in carcinoid syndrome.
High blood pressure caused by narrowed renal arteries, activating the renin-angiotensin system. Worsens with ACE inhibitors.
A positively charged protein that binds and neutralizes heparin, used for heparin overdose.
An alpha-glucosidase inhibitor that slows carbohydrate absorption in the gut, lowering post-meal glucose. Causes flatulence.
Paired ducts formed by seminal vesicle and vas deferens that pass through the prostate to the urethra.
The hormone feedback system in which hypothalamic GnRH stimulates pituitary LH and FSH to drive sex hormone and gamete production.
An intracellular nuclear receptor activated by progesterone in the uterus and breast. Its expression in breast cancer predicts hormone therapy response.
An antifibrinolytic that blocks plasminogen's lysine binding sites, used for heavy menstrual bleeding and surgical bleeding.
A congenital uterine anomaly with a membranous wall dividing the cavity, causing recurrent miscarriage. The most common structural anomaly.
A congenital defect where the urethral opening is on the upper (dorsal) surface of the penis, associated with bladder exstrophy.
Compression of a peripheral nerve, such as carpal tunnel syndrome, causing pain, numbness and weakness in its distribution.
A long-acting phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor used for erectile dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension. Contraindicated with nitrates.
Paired glands at the vaginal opening that secrete lubricating mucus. Duct blockage causes cysts or abscesses.
The peritoneal recess between the rectum and uterus, the lowest part of the female abdominal cavity, where fluid and abscess collect.
A benign ovarian cyst from an ovarian follicle that fails to rupture or reabsorb, usually resolving on its own.
An aromatase inhibitor used for estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer and to induce ovulation.
A benign fluid-filled ovarian tumor lined by tubal-type epithelium, the most common benign epithelial ovarian tumor.
A benign ovarian germ cell tumor (mature cystic teratoma) containing hair, teeth and skin tissue.
The pregnancy-modified endometrium, formed under progesterone, which the embryo implants in.
A testicular sex cord-stromal tumor secreting androgens, causing gynecomastia, with Reinke crystals on histology.
Waking at night to urinate, as in BPH, heart failure and diabetes.
A protease made by prostate epithelium, raised in prostate cancer, BPH and prostatitis. Used for screening and follow-up of prostate cancer.
